stem: In React 19, when does the function passed to `useEffect` run after a component renders?

options.text: During rendering, right before the component returns its JSX
options.why: Effects never run during render. Render must stay pure, so React defers effects until after the commit.

options.text: After the commit to the DOM, usually once the browser has painted
options.why: Passive effects are scheduled after the commit so they do not block the browser from showing the update.

options.text: Before React updates the DOM, so the effect can change what gets committed
options.why: Nothing runs between render and DOM mutation for you to hook into; layout and passive effects both run after the commit.

options.text: Only when the user interacts with the component, such as on click
options.why: That describes event handlers. Effects run because rendering happened, not because of a specific interaction.

explanation: React renders, commits the changes to the DOM, and then runs passive effects (`useEffect`), normally after the browser has had a chance to paint. Use `useLayoutEffect` only when you must read or change layout before paint.

stem: Assigning a new value to `ref.current` (from `useRef`) inside an event handler causes the component to re-render.

options.text: True
options.why: Refs are plain mutable boxes. React does not watch them, so changing one schedules no render.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: changing `ref.current` never triggers a render. Use state when the UI must reflect the value.

explanation: A ref is a stable object whose `current` property you can read and write freely in handlers and effects. Because React does not track it, the screen will not update when it changes. That makes refs right for timer IDs, DOM nodes and "latest value" storage, and wrong for anything that should appear in the UI.

options.text: It runs once after the first render and never again
options.why: That is the behaviour of an empty array `[]`, not of an omitted one.

options.text: It runs after every committed render of the component
options.why: With no array, React has nothing to compare, so the effect re-runs after each commit.

options.text: React infers the dependencies from the variables used in the body
options.why: React does no inference at runtime. The lint rule suggests dependencies, but only the array you pass counts.

options.text: It throws, because the dependency array is a required argument
options.why: The array is optional; leaving it out is valid and simply means "after every render".

explanation: Omitted array: run after every render. `[]`: run after mount only (plus the extra dev-only StrictMode cycle). `[a, b]`: run after mount and whenever `a` or `b` changes by `Object.is`. Updating `document.title` on every render is cheap, so omitting the array is acceptable here, though `[count]` states the intent better.

stem: Match each piece of code with when it runs relative to rendering and painting.

options.text: Before any layout effects, while the DOM mutations are being applied
options.why: Insertion effects run first so styles exist before layout is read.

options.text: After DOM mutations, synchronously, before the browser paints
options.why: Layout effects block paint.

options.text: After the commit, usually after the browser paints
options.why: Passive effects do not block paint.

options.text: Only in response to a specific user interaction
options.why: Event handlers are not tied to rendering.

prompts.text: `useEffect` callback that connects to a chat server

explanation: Within one commit React runs insertion effects, then layout effects, then (later) passive effects. Insertion effects exist for libraries that inject `<style>` tags; layout effects are for measuring and adjusting layout without flicker; passive effects are the default for synchronising with external systems. Event handlers run only when the event fires.

stem: A component that uses both `useEffect` and `useLayoutEffect` is rendered on the server with `renderToString` (React 19). What happens to its effects?

options.text: Both effects run once on the server after the HTML string is produced
options.why: There is no DOM or commit on the server, so React has nothing to run effects against.

options.text: `useLayoutEffect` runs on the server and `useEffect` waits for the client
options.why: Neither runs on the server. Layout effects need real layout, which only the browser has.

options.text: Neither runs on the server; they run in the browser after hydration
options.why: Server rendering produces HTML only. Effects belong to the client commit.

options.text: React throws, because effects are not allowed in server-rendered components
options.why: Effects are allowed in client components that are server-rendered; they are simply skipped there.

explanation: Server rendering calls your component to produce HTML and stops. Effects run on the client once the component hydrates. React 19 also dropped the old warning about `useLayoutEffect` during server rendering. Code that must touch `window`, `document` or `localStorage` therefore belongs in an effect or an event handler, not in render.

stem: To get a DOM node into an effect, you create a ref object with which hook and pass it to the element's `ref` attribute? Type the hook name.
explanation: `const inputRef = useRef(null)` plus `<input ref={inputRef} />` makes React set `inputRef.current` to the DOM node during commit, so it is available in layout and passive effects (and in handlers). It is `null` during the first render because the node does not exist yet.
reference: react.dev: Manipulating the DOM with refs

stem: Which of these is the clearest legitimate use of `useEffect`?

options.text: Computing `fullName` from the `firstName` and `lastName` props
options.why: Derived values should be calculated during render. An effect adds an extra render with stale data first.

options.text: Opening a WebSocket to a chat room and closing it on cleanup
options.why: That synchronises the component with an external system, which is exactly what effects are for.

options.text: Sending a purchase request when the user clicks "Buy"
options.why: That is caused by a specific interaction, so it belongs in the click handler, not in an effect.

options.text: Sorting a list prop before it is rendered
options.why: Sorting is a pure computation. Do it during render, with `useMemo` if it is expensive.

explanation: Effects are an escape hatch for keeping a component in sync with something outside React: network connections, subscriptions, timers, browser APIs and non-React widgets. Pure calculations belong in render, and work triggered by a particular event belongs in that event's handler.
reference: react.dev: You Might Not Need an Effect

options.text: `mount`
options.why: That is what production logs. In development StrictMode adds one extra setup and cleanup cycle on mount.

options.text: `mount`, `cleanup`, `mount`
options.why: StrictMode runs setup, then cleanup, then setup again to prove the cleanup undoes the setup.

options.text: `mount`, `mount`
options.why: React never runs setup twice without the cleanup in between; that would leak resources.

options.text: `mount`, `mount`, `cleanup`, `cleanup`
options.why: The extra cycle is setup, cleanup, setup. Cleanup at the end only runs when the component really unmounts.

explanation: In development StrictMode simulates an immediate unmount and remount for every newly mounted component. Effects that open something must close it in cleanup, so the second setup leaves the system in the same state as a single one. This never happens in production builds.
reference: react.dev: StrictMode (fixing bugs found by re-running Effects)

options.text: It counts 1, 2, 3, … as intended
options.why: The interval callback is created once and keeps reading `count` from the first render, where it is 0.

options.text: It stays at 0 forever because the interval never fires
options.why: The interval does fire; each tick calls `setCount(0 + 1)`.

options.text: It shows 0, then 1, and stays at 1
options.why: Every tick sets the state to `0 + 1`, so after the first change React bails out on identical values.

options.text: It goes 0, 1, 0, 1 as the stale and fresh values alternate
options.why: There is only one interval and it always sets 1; nothing ever sets the count back to 0.

explanation: With `[]` the effect runs once, so its interval closure captures `count = 0` from the first render. Each tick calls `setCount(1)`. After the first update the value is already 1, so later calls change nothing. Fix it with the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)`, which does not depend on the captured value.

stem: Using the counter from the stale-interval example (`setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)` inside `useEffect(..., [])`), which two changes make it count correctly? (Choose two.)

options.text: Call `setCount(c => c + 1)` inside the interval and keep the `[]` dependency array
options.why: The updater receives the latest state, so the callback no longer needs the stale `count`.

options.text: Keep `setCount(count + 1)` and change the dependency array to `[count]`
options.why: The effect now re-subscribes on every change, so each new interval sees the current count. It works, but resets the timer each tick.

options.text: Remove the cleanup so the interval is not cleared between renders
options.why: The effect still only runs once, so the closure is still stale. Removing cleanup just risks leaking intervals.

options.text: Wrap the interval callback in `useMemo` so it is recalculated each render
options.why: `useMemo` cannot be used inside an effect, and recalculating a function does not change the interval that was already registered.

options.text: Store the count in a ref instead of state and keep calling `setCount`
options.why: If the displayed value lives in a ref, updates to it never re-render, so the screen would not change.

explanation: The bug is a stale closure. Either stop reading `count` in the callback (the updater form, usually best) or make the effect re-run when `count` changes so the closure is refreshed. The second fix tears down and recreates the interval every second, which can drift; the updater form keeps one interval for the component's whole life.

options.text: Once, because `options` always has the same content
options.why: React compares dependencies with `Object.is`, which checks identity, not structure.

options.text: Three times: the mount and each of the two later renders
options.why: Each render builds a new `options` object, so the dependency changes every time.

options.text: Twice, because React skips the effect when only object contents match
options.why: React never compares object contents, so no render is skipped.

options.text: Zero times, because objects are not allowed in the dependency array
options.why: Objects are allowed; they just compare by reference.

explanation: A fresh object literal is a different reference on every render, so `Object.is(prev, next)` is false and the effect unsubscribes and resubscribes each time (verified: three renders, three runs). Move the object inside the effect, or depend on its primitive fields (`[id]`).

stem: Which of these jobs should usually NOT be done in an effect? (Choose three.)

options.text: Filtering a list prop by a search term before rendering it
options.why: That is derived data. Compute it during render instead of storing it in state from an effect.

options.text: Resetting all of a form's state when its `userId` prop changes
options.why: Give the component `key={userId}` instead; React then starts it fresh without an extra render.

options.text: Posting an analytics "purchase" event because the user clicked "Buy"
options.why: The cause is the click, so the logic belongs in the click handler.

options.text: Subscribing to the browser `resize` event and removing the listener on cleanup
options.why: That synchronises with a browser API, which is a proper use of an effect.

options.text: Connecting to a chat server for the current `roomId`
options.why: Keeping a connection in sync with props is the textbook effect.

explanation: Effects synchronise with external systems. Data you can compute from props and state belongs in render, a full reset belongs to a `key`, and work caused by a specific interaction belongs in its handler. Each misuse costs at least one extra render and often shows stale UI first.
reference: react.dev: You Might Not Need an Effect

options.text: It renders 0, then 1, and stops because React deduplicates the update
options.why: Each render produces a new `n`, so `n + 1` is always a new value and nothing is deduplicated.

options.text: It keeps re-rendering, and React logs "Maximum update depth exceeded"
options.why: Every render runs the effect, which sets new state, which renders again, without end.

options.text: React throws immediately during the first render, so nothing is shown
options.why: The update happens in an effect, after commit, so the first render succeeds. The loop starts afterwards.

options.text: Nothing happens, because state updates inside effects are ignored
options.why: Effects can update state; that is how this loop forms.

explanation: With no dependency array the effect runs after every render, and it always sets a new value. React detects long chains of nested updates from effects and logs "Maximum update depth exceeded. This can happen when a component calls setState inside useEffect…", but the loop itself keeps burning CPU. Add dependencies, or compute the value during render instead.

stem: `<ChatRoom roomId="a" />` is mounted, and its effect connects to `roomId` with cleanup `disconnect(roomId)`. The parent then renders `<ChatRoom roomId="b" />`. Put what happens in order.

options.text: React calls `ChatRoom` with `roomId = "b"` and commits the result
options.why: Rendering comes first.

options.text: The previous cleanup runs: `disconnect("a")`
options.why: Cleanup uses values from the render that created it.

options.text: The new effect runs: `connect("b")`
options.why: The new effect sees the new props.

explanation: When a dependency changes, React first renders and commits with the new props, then runs the old effect's cleanup (with the old closure, so `"a"`), then the new effect (with `"b"`). Verified in React 19.3: `connect a, disconnect a, connect b`.

stem: When `roomId` changes from `"a"` to `"b"`, the cleanup function of the previous effect run still sees `roomId === "a"`.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: each cleanup closes over the props and state of the render that created it.

options.text: False
options.why: The cleanup is a closure from the earlier render, so it does not see the new props.

explanation: Every render has its own props, state and functions. The cleanup returned by the `"a"` render therefore disconnects from `"a"`, which is exactly what you want. Verified with React 19.3: switching from `a` to `b` logs `disconnect a` before `connect b`.

options.text: Change the dependency array to `[]` so only one request is ever sent
options.why: Then switching users never fetches B at all, which swaps a race for stale data.

options.text: Set `let ignore = false`, return `() => { ignore = true }`, and only call `setUser` when `!ignore`
options.why: The cleanup marks the earlier request as stale, so its late response is dropped.

options.text: Wrap `setUser` in `startTransition` so React applies results in order
options.why: Transitions mark updates as non-urgent. They do not reorder or cancel network responses.

options.text: Move the fetch into `useLayoutEffect` so it finishes before paint
options.why: A layout effect starts the request earlier, but the response still arrives asynchronously in any order.

explanation: Responses can arrive in a different order from the requests. Because cleanup runs before the next effect, a flag set in cleanup tells the older request it is no longer current. `AbortController` additionally cancels the request itself. Data-fetching libraries and framework loaders handle this for you, which is why React recommends them.

stem: An effect creates an `AbortController`, passes `controller.signal` to `fetch`, and calls `controller.abort()` in cleanup. The dependency changes while a request is in flight. What happens to that request's promise?

options.text: It resolves normally, and React discards the result automatically
options.why: React knows nothing about your fetch. You must handle the aborted promise yourself.

options.text: It stays pending forever, which leaks memory
options.why: Aborting settles the promise; it does not leave it pending.

options.text: It rejects with an `AbortError`, which the code should catch
options.why: Aborting rejects the fetch with a DOMException named `AbortError`.

options.text: The browser retries it once the new effect has run
options.why: Browsers do not retry aborted fetches; the request is simply cancelled.

explanation: Abort both cancels the network request and rejects the `fetch` promise with an `AbortError`. Without a `catch` that ignores it (for example `if (e.name !== "AbortError") setError(e)`), the cancelled request shows up as an error or an unhandled rejection. In StrictMode development you will see the first request aborted every time.

stem: A component has `useEffect(fn, [a])`. It mounts with `a = 1` and then re-renders with `a` equal to 1, 2, 2 and 3. How many times does the effect run in total, including the mount? Type a number.
explanation: It runs on mount (1), skips the render where `a` stays 1, runs when `a` becomes 2 (2), skips the second 2, and runs for 3 (3). React compares each dependency with the previous render's value using `Object.is`. Verified in React 19.3.

options.text: `render Parent`
options.why: Rendering starts at the top.

options.text: `render Child`
options.why: Children render after their parent.

options.text: `effect Child`
options.why: Effects run bottom-up.

options.text: `effect Parent`
options.why: The parent's effect runs last.

explanation: Rendering walks the tree top-down, but effects run in a post-order traversal: children before parents. That way a parent's effect can rely on its children's effects (and refs) already being set up. Verified in React 19.3: `render P, render C, effect C, effect P`.

stem: With the same `Parent`/`Child` pair, each effect now also returns a cleanup that logs `cleanup Parent` or `cleanup Child`. The whole tree is then unmounted. In React 19, what is logged?

options.text: `cleanup Child`, then `cleanup Parent`
options.why: That mirrors the mount order, but React 19 runs unmount cleanups top-down.

options.text: `cleanup Parent`, then `cleanup Child`
options.why: When a subtree is deleted, React runs cleanups as it walks down from the removed root.

options.text: Only `cleanup Parent`, because a child's cleanup is skipped when its parent unmounts
options.why: Every mounted effect's cleanup runs on unmount, including the child's.

options.text: The order is random and depends on scheduling
options.why: The order is deterministic; it follows the tree traversal.

explanation: This trips up many developers. Setup runs children first, but on deletion React visits the removed subtree from the top and runs cleanups as it goes, so the parent's cleanup runs before the child's (verified in React 19.3: `cleanup P, cleanup C`). Don't write cleanups that assume a child has already torn down.

stem: Both `Parent` and `Child` have effects with no dependency array, each logging setup and cleanup. The parent re-renders. Which log order does React 19 produce after the renders?

options.text: `cleanup Child`, `effect Child`, `cleanup Parent`, `effect Parent` (one component at a time)
options.why: React does not interleave per component. It runs every pending cleanup before any new setup.

options.text: `cleanup Child`, `cleanup Parent`, `effect Child`, `effect Parent`
options.why: All cleanups run first (children first), then all new effects (children first).

options.text: `cleanup Parent`, `cleanup Child`, `effect Parent`, `effect Child`
options.why: Updates use the bottom-up order; the top-down order is only for subtree deletion.

options.text: `effect Child`, `effect Parent`, `cleanup Child`, `cleanup Parent`
options.why: A new effect never runs before the previous cleanup of the same effect.

explanation: For an update, React first runs every passive cleanup that needs to run across the tree, then every new passive effect. Both passes go child before parent. Verified in React 19.3: `cleanup C, cleanup P, effect C, effect P`. So by the time any new effect runs, all old subscriptions are already gone.

options.text: `layout 1`, `passive 1`, `layout 2`, `passive 2` (one component at a time)
options.why: React does not finish one component before the next. It runs each effect phase across the whole tree.

options.text: `layout 1`, `layout 2`, `passive 1`, `passive 2`
options.why: All layout effects run in the commit, then all passive effects run later.

options.text: `passive 1`, `passive 2`, `layout 1`, `layout 2`
options.why: Layout effects always run before passive effects in the same commit.

options.text: `layout 2`, `layout 1`, `passive 2`, `passive 1`
options.why: Siblings run in tree order, so the first sibling comes first.

explanation: A commit runs phases across the whole tree: insertion effects, DOM mutations, layout effects for every component, then (after paint, usually) passive effects for every component. Siblings follow tree order. Verified in React 19.3.

stem: A component with `useEffect(() => { log('effect ' + k); return () => log('cleanup ' + k); }, [])` is rendered as `<Panel key="A" k="A" />`, then the parent renders `<Panel key="B" k="B" />`. Its body also logs `render ` + k. What is logged during the update?

options.text: `cleanup A`, `render B`, `effect B`
options.why: React renders the new tree before tearing anything down, so `render B` comes first.

options.text: `render B`, `cleanup A`, `effect B`
options.why: The new component renders, then the commit deletes A (running its cleanup) and runs B's effect.

options.text: `render B`, `effect B`, `cleanup A`
options.why: Cleanups of removed components run before new passive effects.

options.text: `render B` only, because the `[]` effect already ran
options.why: A different key means a new component instance, so its `[]` effect runs on its own mount.

explanation: Changing the key unmounts the old instance and mounts a new one. React renders the new tree first, then commits: the deleted component's cleanup runs, then the new component's effect. Verified in React 19.3: `render B, cleanup A, effect B`. This is why `key` is the idiomatic way to reset a subtree.

options.text: `createConnection` is called during render; moving it into a `useMemo` call fixes it
options.why: It is already called inside the effect. The problem is the function dependency, not where the connection is made.

options.text: `createOptions` is a new function each render; move it inside the effect and depend on `[roomId, serverUrl]`
options.why: Then the effect depends only on primitives and re-runs only when they change.

options.text: Effects cannot have functions as dependencies; the array should simply be `[]`
options.why: Functions can be dependencies. `[]` would hide real changes to `roomId` and keep the connection stale.

options.text: The cleanup runs too early; returning it from a `setTimeout` keeps the connection alive
options.why: The cleanup is correct. Delaying it would leave two connections open at once.

explanation: A function declared in the component body is recreated on every render, so it is a new reference each time and the effect always re-runs (verified: three renders produce three runs). Move it into the effect so only `roomId` and `serverUrl` are dependencies. If the function must live outside, `useCallback` with the right dependencies also works.

options.text: The connection keeps using the `roomId` from the first render
options.why: The effect ran once, so its closure holds the first value forever.

options.text: Changing `roomId` neither closes the old connection nor opens a new one
options.why: With no dependency the effect never re-runs, so it never re-synchronises.

options.text: React notices the missing dependency at runtime and re-runs the effect anyway
options.why: The lint rule is the only check. At runtime React compares exactly the array you pass.

options.text: The effect now runs after every render, because the array is effectively ignored
options.why: An empty array means mount only. It is not ignored.

options.text: The production build fails to compile until the comment is removed
options.why: Lint comments affect only the linter; the build is unaffected.

explanation: Dependencies are not a choice; they describe what the effect reads. Lying about them leaves the effect synchronised with old values. If you want to read a value without reacting to it, use `useEffectEvent` (stable in React 19.2) instead of suppressing the rule.

options.text: Two intervals, because changing `theme` re-runs the effect
options.why: `theme` is read only inside the effect event, so it is not a dependency of the effect.

options.text: One interval, but every tick reports `light`, because the closure is stale
options.why: An effect event always calls the latest version of its function, so it sees the current `theme`.

options.text: One interval; ticks report `light` before the change and `dark` after
options.why: The effect subscribes once, and the effect event reads the latest props whenever it runs.

options.text: It throws, because effect events cannot be called from timers
options.why: Calling an effect event from code started by an effect, such as a timer, is exactly the intended use.

explanation: `useEffectEvent` separates the reactive part (when to subscribe) from the non-reactive part (what to do with the latest values). The interval is created once (verified: 1 subscription) and reports `light`, then `dark`. The rules: call it only from effects or code they start, and don't list it in dependencies.

options.text: Version 1 re-runs the component before its children render, so children never see the stale selection
options.why: React restarts the component immediately when state is set during its own render, before rendering children.

options.text: Version 2 is preferred because setting state during render always throws
options.why: Setting your own component's state during render is allowed when guarded by a condition. It is how React documents this pattern.

options.text: Both versions commit exactly once, so they behave identically
options.why: Version 2 commits the stale selection first and then commits again after the effect runs.

options.text: Version 1 causes an infinite loop, because it sets state on every render
options.why: It sets state only when `items` differs from the stored previous value, so the loop stops after one restart.

explanation: Verified in React 19.3: with version 1, the parent renders twice and the child renders once with the fresh value. With the effect version, the child renders and commits the stale value, then everything renders again. The render-time version is still a niche tool; if you can, use a `key` or derive the value instead of storing it.
reference: react.dev: You Might Not Need an Effect (adjusting state when a prop changes)

stem: Match each symptom with its most likely cause.

options.text: Measuring the DOM in `useEffect` instead of `useLayoutEffect`
options.why: The first paint shows the wrong position.

options.text: An effect with no cleanup, exposed by StrictMode
options.why: The extra dev-only cycle opens a second resource.

options.text: A stale closure from a missing dependency
options.why: The callback keeps an old value.

options.text: An object or function recreated every render used as a dependency
options.why: Identity changes each render.

prompts.text: A tooltip briefly appears in the wrong place, then jumps into position
In development only, the server logs two open connections for one user
A timer keeps logging the search term the user typed first
An analytics subscription is torn down and recreated on every keystroke in an unrelated field

explanation: Each of these is a well-known effect bug with a clear signature. Flicker means the measurement happened after paint. Development-only duplication means a missing cleanup. A frozen value means a stale closure. Re-running on unrelated renders means a dependency whose identity changes every time.

options.text: When the `<div>` unmounts, React calls the cleanup and does not call the ref with `null`
options.why: Returning a cleanup opts out of the old `ref(null)` call.

options.text: On each re-render React calls the previous cleanup, then calls the new ref with the node
options.why: A new function identity means React detaches the old ref and attaches the new one.

options.text: React calls the ref with `null` and also calls the cleanup when the element unmounts
options.why: It is one or the other. With a cleanup returned, React skips the `null` call.

options.text: Returning a function from a ref callback is ignored, as it was in React 18
options.why: React 18 ignored it; React 19 treats the return value as a cleanup.

options.text: The ref runs once per mount, no matter how many times the component re-renders
options.why: Only a stable callback (for example from `useCallback`) runs once. An inline one is re-attached each render.

explanation: Verified with React 19.3: mounting logs `ref node`, a re-render logs `ref cleanup, ref node`, and unmounting logs only `ref cleanup`. Without a returned cleanup, unmount calls the ref with `null` instead. In StrictMode development React also double-invokes ref callbacks on mount: `ref node, ref cleanup, ref node`.

options.text: Effects cannot call functions received as props
options.why: Effects can call props. The problem is when and how many times the update happens.

options.text: The child commits first and the parent updates afterwards, adding a render pass and in-between UI
options.why: The parent's state changes one commit later than it needed to, so both components render twice.

options.text: `onChange` runs before the input's state has updated, so the parent always receives the previous query
options.why: The effect runs after commit, so it sees the new `query`; the problem is the extra pass, not a stale value.

options.text: It only fails in StrictMode, where the effect runs twice
options.why: StrictMode makes it run twice in development, but the timing and extra render happen in production too.

explanation: When a change starts from an event, update everything in that handler: `setQuery(v); onChange(v);`. React batches both updates into one render. Routing the notification through an effect makes the parent learn about it one commit late, and the effect also re-runs whenever the parent passes a new `onChange` function. Lifting the state up is often better still.
reference: react.dev: You Might Not Need an Effect (notifying parent components)

stem: In a production build, components inside `<StrictMode>` still run their effects twice on mount (setup, cleanup, setup).

options.text: True
options.why: StrictMode's extra checks, including the effect re-run, are development-only.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: production runs each effect once per mount, whether or not StrictMode is present.

explanation: StrictMode adds development-only checks: double-invoking component bodies and initialisers, re-running effects, double-invoking ref callbacks and warning about deprecated APIs. None of these happen in production, so seeing duplicate requests only in development is expected and not a production bug.

options.text: It adds a new listener each time without removing the old ones, so Enter calls `save` six times
options.why: The cleanup removes the previous listener before the next effect adds one.

options.text: It removes and re-adds the listener on each change; at any moment exactly one listener holds the current `count`
options.why: Correct, but the re-subscription is wasted work that `useEffectEvent` can avoid.

options.text: It keeps saving `0`, because event listeners capture the value from the first render
options.why: Each re-run registers a new handler that closes over the new `count`.

options.text: It throws, because the same function cannot be passed to both add and remove
options.why: `onKey` in a given closure is the same function object in both calls, which is what removal needs.

explanation: This is correct but churns: every change tears down and re-adds the listener. Wrapping the handler logic in `useEffectEvent(() => save(count))` lets the effect subscribe once with `[]` while still saving the latest count. Without cleanup, listeners would pile up.

stem: Which two effects keep working correctly when StrictMode runs setup, cleanup and setup again in development? (Choose two.)

options.text: `useEffect(() => { const c = connect(); return () => c.disconnect(); }, [])`
options.why: Cleanup disconnects, so after the second setup exactly one connection remains.

options.text: `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(tick, 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])`
options.why: The first interval is cleared, so only one keeps running.

options.text: `useEffect(() => { map.addMarker(pos); }, [])` with no cleanup
options.why: The second setup adds a duplicate marker because nothing removed the first.

options.text: `useEffect(() => { if (!didInit.current) { didInit.current = true; init(); } }, [])` with a ref guard
options.why: The ref skips the second run, which hides missing cleanup instead of fixing it and breaks after real remounts. It is the workaround React discourages.

options.text: `useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll); }, [])`
options.why: No cleanup means two scroll listeners after the dev re-run.

explanation: The question StrictMode asks is: does setup → cleanup → setup leave the system the same as one setup? That holds when cleanup undoes setup. One-time app initialisation belongs outside components (module scope, or a module-level flag), not behind a per-component ref that also skips remounts in production.
reference: react.dev: Synchronizing with Effects (how to handle the Effect firing twice)

options.text: One request and one `setData`, because StrictMode deduplicates identical effects
options.why: StrictMode does not deduplicate. It really runs the setup twice.

options.text: Two requests and two `setData` calls, one per effect run
options.why: The first run's cleanup sets its `ignore` to true, so its response is dropped.

options.text: Two requests; `setData` runs once, with the response of the second effect run
options.why: The first effect is cleaned up before its response arrives, so only the second one applies.

options.text: Two requests, but `setData` never runs, because both effects were cleaned up
options.why: Only the first run was cleaned up. The second is still active when its response arrives.

explanation: StrictMode runs setup (request 1), cleanup (`ignore = true` for request 1), then setup again (request 2). Request 1 resolves into a closure whose flag is set, so it is ignored. Request 2 applies. Verified in React 19.3: 2 calls, 1 applied. In production only one request is sent. Use `AbortController` to also cancel request 1 on the network.

options.text: render w=0, layout w=0, render w=100, layout w=100, passive w=100 (first passive effect skipped)
options.why: The first render's passive effect is not skipped. React flushes it before re-rendering.

options.text: render w=0, layout w=0, passive w=0, render w=100, layout w=100, passive w=100
options.why: The layout update is synchronous, so React first flushes pending passive effects and then re-renders before paint.

options.text: render w=0, layout w=0, passive w=0, passive w=100, render w=100, layout w=100
options.why: An effect cannot run for a render that has not happened yet.

options.text: render w=0, render w=100, layout w=100, passive w=100
options.why: The first commit happens and runs its layout effect; otherwise nothing would call `setW(100)`.

explanation: A state update inside a layout effect is processed synchronously, before the browser paints. Before React starts that synchronous render, it flushes the passive effects still pending from the first commit, so `passive w=0` appears. Then it renders and commits with 100. Verified in React 19.3. The user never sees `w=0` painted, which is why `useLayoutEffect` fixes measurement flicker.

stem: One component uses `useInsertionEffect`, `useLayoutEffect` and `useEffect`, all without dependency arrays and all with cleanups. It re-renders. Put the six callbacks in the order React 19 runs them.

options.text: Insertion effect cleanup
options.why: Insertion effects come first.

options.text: Insertion effect setup
options.why: Runs straight after its cleanup.

options.text: Layout effect cleanup
options.why: Runs during the mutation phase.

options.text: Layout effect setup
options.why: Runs before paint.

options.text: Passive effect cleanup
options.why: Runs after the commit.

options.text: Passive effect setup
options.why: Runs last.

explanation: Insertion effects run during the mutation phase so styles are injected before anything reads layout. Layout cleanups also run during mutation, and new layout effects run once the DOM is updated, still before paint. Passive cleanups and setups run afterwards. Verified in React 19.3: `insertion cleanup, insertion, layout cleanup, layout, passive cleanup, passive`.

stem: Two siblings `<X n={1} />` and `<X n={2} />` each have a `useLayoutEffect` with cleanup and no dependency array. Their parent re-renders. Which statement about the layout callbacks is true?

options.text: React runs `cleanup 1, layout 1, cleanup 2, layout 2`, finishing each sibling before the next
options.why: Effect phases are not done per component. Every layout cleanup happens before any new layout effect.

options.text: All layout cleanups run first: `cleanup 1, cleanup 2, layout 1, layout 2`
options.why: Layout cleanups run in the mutation phase and new layout effects in the later layout phase.

options.text: The cleanups run in reverse order, `cleanup 2, cleanup 1`, so the last mounted is torn down first
options.why: Cleanups follow tree order, not reverse order.

options.text: Layout cleanups are deferred and run with the passive cleanups after paint
options.why: Layout cleanups run synchronously in the commit, before paint.

explanation: Verified in React 19.3: `layout cleanup 1`, `layout cleanup 2`, then `layout 1`, `layout 2` (with insertion effects interleaved during mutation). The guarantee is that no new layout effect sees a half-torn-down sibling, which matters when siblings share a resource such as a global listener or a measuring element.

stem: In development under `<StrictMode>`, `Parent` renders `<Child />`. Each has a `[]` effect logging setup and cleanup. What is logged on mount?

options.text: effect Child, cleanup Child, effect Child, effect Parent, cleanup Parent, effect Parent (each component separately)
options.why: StrictMode does not re-run each component's effects individually; it simulates unmounting and remounting the whole new tree.

options.text: effect Child, effect Parent, cleanup Parent, cleanup Child, effect Child, effect Parent
options.why: Normal mount, then a simulated unmount (top-down cleanups), then a remount (bottom-up setups).

options.text: effect Parent, effect Child, cleanup Child, cleanup Parent, effect Parent, effect Child
options.why: Setups always run children first, including during the StrictMode remount.

options.text: effect Child, effect Parent
options.why: That is the production log. StrictMode adds the extra cycle in development.

explanation: StrictMode mounts normally (children first), then simulates removing the tree, which runs cleanups parent first as on a real unmount, then mounts again (children first). Verified in React 19.3. This combines the bottom-up order of setups with the top-down order of deletions.

stem: Which two statements about `useEffectEvent` (stable in React 19.2) are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Calling the returned function during render throws an error
options.why: React throws "A function wrapped in useEffectEvent can't be called during rendering."

options.text: It must not be listed in the effect's dependency array
options.why: Its identity is intentionally unstable; the linter knows to leave it out.

options.text: It returns a stable function you can pass to child components as an `onClick` prop
options.why: Effect events are meant to be called from effects only; passing them to children is unsupported.

options.text: Values it reads become dependencies, so the effect re-runs when they change
options.why: The opposite: reading a value in an effect event keeps it out of the effect's dependencies.

options.text: It is the recommended replacement for `useCallback` on JSX event handlers
options.why: Normal handlers in JSX already see the latest values; `useEffectEvent` solves an effect-only problem.

explanation: An effect event is logic that is triggered by an effect but should see the latest props and state without re-triggering that effect. Verified with React 19.3: calling it during render throws. It should be declared next to the effect that uses it and called only from that effect or from callbacks the effect sets up (timers, listeners, connections).

stem: A component has `useEffect(fn, [a])`. It mounts with `a = NaN`, then re-renders with `a` equal to `NaN`, then `0`, then `-0`. How many times does the effect run in total, including the mount? Type a number.
explanation: React compares dependencies with `Object.is`. `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true, so the second render skips. `Object.is(NaN, 0)` is false (run 2), and `Object.is(0, -0)` is false (run 3), even though `0 === -0`. Verified in React 19.3: 3 runs. This rarely matters in practice, but it shows that the comparison is `Object.is`, not `===`.

stem: Two components unmount together: siblings `<X n={1} />` and `<X n={2} />`, each with a layout effect and a passive effect that both have cleanups. Which statement describes the cleanup order?

options.text: Each component runs its passive cleanup and then its layout cleanup before the next component starts
options.why: Passive cleanups are not run per component during deletion. They are collected and run after the layout phase.

options.text: Both layout cleanups run synchronously first; both passive cleanups run afterwards
options.why: Layout (and insertion) cleanups run during the mutation phase; passive cleanups run later.

options.text: Passive cleanups run first, because passive effects were set up last
options.why: Cleanup order is by phase, not by the reverse of setup time.

options.text: Only layout cleanups run; passive cleanups are skipped for unmounted components
options.why: Every passive cleanup still runs on unmount.

explanation: Verified in React 19.3: `insertion cleanup 1, layout cleanup 1, insertion cleanup 2, layout cleanup 2`, then `passive cleanup 1, passive cleanup 2`. Layout cleanups must run before the DOM is removed, so they are synchronous; passive cleanups can wait. Don't rely on a passive cleanup running before the DOM nodes disappear.

options.text: Layout effects run before the DOM is updated, so the first render already has the height
options.why: Layout effects run after the DOM is updated. That is why they can measure.

options.text: It reads layout without forcing the browser to calculate styles, so it is faster than `useEffect`
options.why: Measuring forces layout either way. The difference is timing relative to paint, not cost.

options.text: The state update inside it re-renders synchronously before paint, so the wrong position is never shown; it blocks painting
options.why: React processes the update before the browser paints, at the cost of delaying that paint.

options.text: Layout effects batch with the browser's next animation frame, so both positions render in one frame
options.why: No frame is shared. React simply finishes the corrected render before the browser paints.

explanation: `useEffect` usually runs after paint, so the browser shows the first position before the corrected render arrives. A state update inside `useLayoutEffect` is handled synchronously before paint (see the w=0/w=100 trace), so only the final position is painted. The cost is that heavy work there delays the frame, so keep layout effects for measuring and positioning.
reference: react.dev: useLayoutEffect (measuring layout before the browser repaints)

stem: A parent renders `<Profile user={{ id, name }} />`, building a new object on every render. Inside `Profile`, `useEffect(() => loadPosts(user.id), [user])` refetches on every parent render. Which two changes stop the needless refetches? (Choose two.)

options.text: In `Profile`, depend on the primitive: `const { id } = user;` and `[id]`
options.why: The effect now compares a number or string, which stays equal across renders.

options.text: In the parent, memoise the object with `useMemo(() => ({ id, name }), [id, name])`
options.why: The prop keeps the same identity until `id` or `name` actually changes.

options.text: Wrap `Profile` in `React.memo`
options.why: `memo` compares props shallowly, and the `user` object is new each time, so it still re-renders and refetches.

options.text: Use `JSON.stringify(user)` as the only dependency and keep reading `user.id` inside
options.why: It avoids identity churn, but now the effect reads `user` without listing it, which the lint rule flags and can hide stale values. Prefer the primitive.

options.text: Replace `useEffect` with `useLayoutEffect`
options.why: Timing is not the problem. The dependency still changes every render.

explanation: The trigger is a dependency whose identity changes every render. Fix it where the object is made (memoise it) or where it is consumed (depend on the primitive fields you actually read). Depending on `user.id` is usually best because it states exactly when the data should reload. The React Compiler can memoise the parent object automatically.
reference: react.dev: Removing Effect dependencies (do you want to read a value without reacting?)

options.text: Keep the handler as is and change the dependencies to `[socket]`
options.why: The handler would then always use the first `muted` value, a stale closure.

options.text: `const onMessage = useEffectEvent(m => { if (!muted) play(m); });` and subscribe with `socket.on('message', onMessage)` and `[socket]`
options.why: The subscription depends only on `socket`, and the effect event reads the current `muted`.

options.text: Wrap the handler in `useCallback(..., [muted])` and depend on `[socket, handler]`
options.why: The callback changes whenever `muted` changes, so the effect still re-subscribes.

options.text: Store `muted` in state and read it with `setMuted(m => m)` inside the handler
options.why: An updater must be pure and is not a way to read state; it can also trigger extra renders.

explanation: `muted` affects what the handler does but not whether you should be subscribed, which makes it a non-reactive value. `useEffectEvent` gives you that split: the effect re-runs only when `socket` changes, and every call sees the latest `muted`. Before 19.2 the usual workaround was a "latest ref" updated in a layout effect.

options.text: Refs cannot be assigned during render; React throws a runtime error
options.why: React does not throw, but writing to refs during render breaks its rules for pure rendering.

options.text: A render can be thrown away or repeated, so a write during render can leave the ref holding a callback from a render that never committed
options.why: With concurrent rendering and StrictMode, renders can be discarded or run twice, so render-time writes are unsafe.

options.text: Assigning in render triggers an extra re-render, doubling the work
options.why: Writing a ref never schedules a render.

options.text: The interval would capture the ref object from the first render and never see later values
options.why: The ref object is stable, and `latest.current` is read when each tick runs, so that part works.

explanation: Render must be pure: React may render a component, interrupt it or discard the result (transitions, Suspense, StrictMode). If you write to a ref during such a render, the interval can call a callback from UI that never appeared. Updating the ref in a layout effect means it only changes for committed renders. `useEffectEvent` now packages this pattern safely.
reference: react.dev: useRef (do not write or read ref.current during rendering)
